Prebuilt **Linux and Windows x86-64** binaries of `k3`, the pure-C Kimi K3 inference
engine from [FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c](https://github.com/FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c),
built with the Tiny C Compiler (TCC) only.

**This release makes Windows and Linux compute the same bits.** Through
[v1.2.3](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/releases/tag/v1.2.3), `expf` and `tanhf`
came from each platform's C library, and Windows (`msvcrt.dll`) and Linux (glibc)
rounded them differently on some inputs. The engine now uses its own correctly rounded
versions, so the same prompt and weights give the same floats on both.

## What changed

- **New `k3_expf` and `k3_tanhf`.** Each returns the float nearest to the exact
  mathematical value (ties to even). Only one such float exists, so every correct
  implementation on every platform must return it. They are written in plain C double
  arithmetic: no C library call, no `fma`, no `long double`.
- **Where they are used:** SiTU-GLU, ShortConv, the KDA decay, the attention softmax,
  the attention gate and the MoE router. The matrix kernels, the KDA step and rmsnorm
  were already bit-identical across platforms and are unchanged.
- **Results no longer depend on the glibc version either.** Different glibc releases
  round `tanhf` differently, too.

## Output differs slightly from v1.2.3

On Linux, glibc 2.39's `tanhf` is not correctly rounded on 2.8% of all float inputs
(118,674,314 of 2^32), and its `expf` on 170,648. On Windows, `msvcrt.dll` is off on
some inputs as well. Where an activation hits one of those inputs, it now moves by one
unit in the last place. The reference tests still match exactly, but text generated from
real weights can diverge from v1.2.3 after many tokens. Neither version is "wrong"; this
one is exact and the same everywhere.

## How it was verified

- **Every input.** `tools/check_math.c` ran both functions on all 2^32 float inputs.
  - Reference: glibc's long double `expl` and `tanhl`, with a 2^-56 safety margin.
  - Result: **0 failures**, and **0 cases** close enough to a rounding boundary to need
    the 300-bit settler, `tools/check_math_exact.py`.
  - A further 5,970 random results match a 300-bit computation directly.
  - The check caught one bug during development, `tanh(-0)` returning +0, which was
    fixed before this release.
- **Same bits on Windows.** A new test, `tests/unit/test_math.c`, runs on every build on
  both platforms. It checks 72 known answers from a 300-bit computation and a digest of
  both functions over 17 million inputs. Windows and Linux CI produce the same digest,
  `5c7379a2bb2338de`.
- **Same kernel output on both platforms.** In the CI benchmark, the three kernels that
  used to differ now print the same output digests on `windows-latest` and
  `ubuntu-latest`: SiTU-GLU `7ed17a241cc2e6ff`, ShortConv `00f49b5db097773d`, KDA decay
  `e3fc484de314e27b`.
- **Full suite on each OS before packaging:** `22 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped`,
  `VERDICT: ENGINE MATCHES THE REFERENCE EXACTLY`, `ALL WEIGHTLESS TESTS PASSED`.
- **Not verified:** inference on real Kimi K3 weights with this release, on either
  platform.

## Speed

Correct rounding costs a little more than the C library. The new functions take a cheap
path for almost every input, and the proven exact path only when a result lies very
close to a rounding boundary. The code is written around how TCC compiles: few
statements, no signed division, no function call for the sigmoid.

Windows build, run back to back on one 4-core Xeon under Wine (best of 7 per run, three
runs each, in microseconds per call):

| Kernel | v1.2.3 | v1.3.0 |
|---|---|---|
| SiTU-GLU 3072 | 149 / 183 / 189 | 232 / 256 / 266 |
| ShortConv 36864 | 1680 / 1697 / 1713 | 1761 / 1857 / 1857 |
| KDA decay 96x128 | 599 / 613 / 670 | 648 / 668 / 785 |

- **ShortConv and the KDA decay:** about the same as v1.2.3, within this machine's noise.
- **SiTU-GLU:** about 1.4x slower, roughly 0.1 s more per token on one thread. The matrix
  kernels take about 30-40 s per token on one thread, so the total is well under 1%.
- **Caveat:** Wine's `msvcrt` is not Microsoft's, so v1.2.3's real Windows timings may
  differ somewhat. The matrix kernels are unchanged.

## Downloads

| File | Runs on |
|---|---|
| `k3-1.3.0-windows-x64.zip` | 64-bit Windows Vista or later, any x86-64 CPU |
| `k3-1.3.0-linux-x64.zip` | 64-bit Linux with glibc 2.38 or newer (e.g. Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 39), any x86-64 CPU |
| `SHA256SUMS.txt` | Checksums for both zips |

Each zip contains `k3` (`k3.exe` on Windows), `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and `README.txt`.

- **No installer and no extra DLLs.**
  - `k3.exe` imports only `kernel32.dll` and `msvcrt.dll`.
  - The Linux `k3` needs only `libc.so.6` and `libm.so.6`.
- **Verify the download:**
  - PowerShell: `Get-FileHash .\k3-1.3.0-windows-x64.zip -Algorithm SHA256`
  - Linux: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing`
- **Quick check:** `k3 --version` should print `k3 1.3.0`.

Running inference needs the Kimi K3 checkpoint (about 1.56 TB), downloaded separately.
See [docs/QUICKSTART.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.3.0/docs/QUICKSTART.md).
To build from source on Windows, run `setup.bat`; see
[docs/BUILD-WINDOWS.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.3.0/docs/BUILD-WINDOWS.md).

## How it was built

[`release.yml`](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.3.0/.github/workflows/release.yml)
on GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` and `windows-latest` runners, with TCC 0.9.28rc (TinyCC
commit `e23dabed`).

Full history: [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/s81/kimi-work-8Gb/blob/v1.3.0/CHANGELOG.md).
